2-7-p023-02.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.SourceFile: Section 3.1 specifies Unicode text in an 8-bit encoding. At version 2.7, `SourceFile` is `True` for every byte sequence, so Unicode validity is outside this predicate. The ASCII byte check is specific to version 2.0.
2-7-p023-02.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Tokenization.From: The token stream in this passage is the output of the relation in `Tokenization.From`. A step splits off whitespace and one token, records its byte offset, leaves the token's source spelling intact, and continues on the rest. The rules require a delimiter after a non-parenthesis token and admit a final comment at end of input.
2-7-p023-02.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.comment: In `|a;b|`, the semicolon is part of the quoted name. A semicolon at a token boundary starts a comment, and the `comment` expression consumes through the first line feed or carriage return. The tokenization rules determine which situation applies.
2-7-p023-02.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.printableChar: The printable character class in this paragraph corresponds to two byte ranges in Lean, $32$ through $126$ and $128$ through $255$. A UTF-8 character can span several bytes, and this regular expression matches one byte at a time.

2-7-p024-01.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Tokenization: In `(assert x)`, the tokens start at byte offsets 0, 1, 8 and 9. The space after `assert` is consumed, leaving a gap in the offsets. `Tokenization` starts the `From` relation at offset zero, so the parser receives tokens that still point to their positions in the original input.
2-7-p024-01.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Tokenization.From: Try splitting `1.5` after `1`. The next byte `.` is outside the allowed delimiters, so that split cannot be a `From.token` step. Taking `1.5` together as a decimal works. This is how the formal delimitation rule keeps one literal from turning into two tokens.
2-7-p024-01.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.categoryRegex: The standard's list of token kinds becomes a case split in `categoryRegex`, with separate cases for simple and quoted symbols. The selected version determines the reserved words and simple-symbol rule, and version 2.0 uses its own string rule.
2-7-p024-01.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.comment: The regex separates an ordinary comment into three pieces. `lit ";"` starts it, `star (minus anyChar lineBreak)` accepts its body, and `lineBreak` consumes the first following line feed or carriage return. Thus when a line starts with `; note`, the line break is consumed with that comment and the text on the next line remains for tokenization. A final comment without a line break is handled by the separate `commentAtEnd` rule.
2-7-p024-01.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.lineBreak: `alt (code 10) (code 13)` matches one byte, a line feed or a carriage return. That byte ends the ordinary semicolon comment.
2-7-p024-01.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.whitespace: In `star (alt whiteSpaceChar comment)`, each repetition consumes either a white space byte or a complete line-terminated comment. Zero repetitions allow an empty separator, and the tokenization relation specifies when a delimiter is required.

2-7-p024-02.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.whiteSpaceChar: The four alternatives in `altAll` are the decimal byte codes for tab, line feed, carriage return and space. A sequence of such bytes is handled by the separate `whitespace` expression.

2-7-p024-03.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.printableChar: `printableChar` matches a byte in $32$ through $126$ or $128$ through $255$, leaving out $127$. Compare the explicit upper bound in Appendix B with “from 128 on” in this paragraph about characters.

2-7-p024-04.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.digit: `range 48 57` matches one ASCII byte, from `0` to `9` inclusive. The numeral and decimal rules use this single-byte class to build longer tokens.

2-7-p024-05.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.letter: The two inclusive ranges in `letter` match one ASCII byte, either `A` through `Z` or `a` through `z`. The definition gives the literal alphabet used in simple symbols.

2-7-p024-06.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.numeral: The first branch admits `0`. The second starts with all nonempty digit strings and subtracts those beginning with `0`, so `10` matches and `01` falls outside the rule. The result is a spelling rule for numeral tokens.

2-7-p024-07.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.decimal: The two occurrences of `numeral` enclose a literal point followed by `star (lit "0")`. The extra zero run makes `0.007` possible on the fractional side, and the final numeral ensures at least one digit follows the point.

2-7-p024-08.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.hexadecimal: The literal prefix is `#x`. The following `plus` requires at least one byte from the digit class or the two letter ranges `A` to `F` and `a` to `f`, as in `#x01Ab`.

2-7-p024-10.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.binary: For the standard's `#b001`, `seq` joins the fixed prefix `#b` to three individual matches of `oneOf "01"`. The `plus` combinator means one or more repetitions, so `#b` alone fails. An input such as `#b102` also fails as a binary token because `2` is outside the repeated class. The rule recognizes the written digits, including their leading zeroes.

2-7-p024-12.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.string: Between the two delimiter quotes, the repeated unit is either one permitted byte other than a quote or the pair `""`. This is the version 2.7 spelling rule on bytes, with the printable byte class in place of a Unicode decoding step.
2-7-p024-12.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.unescape: Strip the outer quotes from `"a""b"` to get `a""b`. Then `unescape` consumes the two adjacent quotes together and emits one, giving the three-character payload `a"b`. This separates the source spelling from the content of the literal.

2-7-p025-04.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.string: A backslash is in the printable byte class used by `string`. Thus `\n` can appear as a backslash followed by `n` in the string interior, while an interior double quote must be written as `""`.
2-7-p025-04.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.unescape: The recursive case for two quote bytes is the only replacement in `unescape`. Given `\x0A` in the interior, it copies the backslash and the next three bytes in order.

2-7-p025-05.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.addedBasicReservedWo: The list on this page is cumulative. In `addedBasicReservedWords` the version 2.7 case contains just `lambda`. `match`, the names for literal categories and the other grammar words come from earlier cases.
2-7-p025-05.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.basicReservedWords: The text `lambda` is a simple symbol in 2.6 and a reserved word in 2.7. `basicReservedWords` accumulates additions through the chosen version, so 2.7 gets the new binder keyword and keeps older ones such as `forall`. A change of version can therefore change a token's category even when its bytes stay the same.
2-7-p025-05.BSmtLibSpec.Parser.Traversal.Received.Of: This parser condition starts with an item already classified as a token or end of input. For a reserved token it tests the union of the version's basic reserved words and command names. All other items satisfy this particular condition.

2-7-p025-08.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.addedCommandNames: The command names are grouped here by the version that introduced them. The 2.7 branch has `declare-sort-parameter` and `define-const`, while the `set-logic` and `set-option` named in the passage come from the 2.0 branch.
2-7-p025-08.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.commandNames: At version 2.7, the concatenation includes the commands added in 2.0, 2.5, 2.6 and 2.7. That is where `define-funs-rec`, which entered the grammar in 2.5, joins the current set of command names.
2-7-p025-08.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.reserved: `litOneOf` matches the complete spelling of a word from either `basicReservedWords` or `commandNames` for that version. This puts a command like `set-option` and a grammar word like `let` in the same lexical category.

2-7-p025-09.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.simpleSymbol: The inner `plus` combines letters, digits and the punctuation listed here into a nonempty candidate. The two subtractions apply the initial-digit and reserved-word exclusions in the continuation below.
2-7-p025-09.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.symbolPunctuation: `oneOf` matches exactly one of the listed punctuation characters. The simple-symbol rule combines that class with letters and digits before checking the whole spelling.

2-7-p025-11.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.simpleSymbol: The nested `minus` expressions remove candidates that start with a digit and candidates whose whole spelling is reserved. For example, `x1` remains a simple symbol in 2.7, while `1x` and `let` are excluded by different subtractions.

2-7-p025-14.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.quotedSymbol: The two outer `lit "|"` expressions are the delimiters. The starred interior permits `||` and strings of printable or white space bytes, with interior bars and backslashes removed from the allowed byte class.

2-7-p026-03.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.Token.content: `abc` and `|abc|` name the same symbol in the standard. `Token.content` gives both the three bytes `abc`, while the grammar token also records whether the spelling was quoted. The lexer can therefore recover the name and still pass on how it appeared in the source.
2-7-p026-03.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.quotedSymbol: The vertical bars let a symbol contain bytes that would divide unquoted tokens. For example, `|two words|` forms a single symbol whose name includes a space. The outer `lit "|"` expressions match the delimiters, and the starred middle part repeats the permitted whitespace or printable bytes after excluding bars and backslashes. The regex checks that spelling. `Token.content` separately removes the delimiters to recover the name bytes.
2-7-p026-03.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.simpleSymbol: The lexical rule can match names beginning with `@` or `.`, including `@abc` and `.abc`. The restriction on who introduces those names concerns solver use, which is outside this spelling test.

2-7-p026-04.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.keyword: Lean accepts `:56` as a keyword, although `56` by itself is a numeral. The keyword rule consumes the colon first and then permits any nonempty run of letters, digits or symbol punctuation. This older rule, retained for 2.7 in the formalization, admits the standard's printed example.

2-7-p026-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SExpr.Valid: Once an S-expression tree is given, `Valid` recurses through its lists to check reserved-word atoms. Each must belong to the selected version's reserved set, and reserved-word atoms are available from 2.6 onward.
2-7-p026-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SExpr.tokens: An atom supplies one syntax token. For a list, Lean joins the members' token lists in order and adds the two parentheses, so an empty list supplies just `(` and `)`.

2-7-p026-07.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SpecConstant: Each alternative has its own Lean constructor with a byte-sequence payload. In particular a numeral stores its digits, and a string stores its content. Their interpretation as terms is supplied by the relevant theory.
2-7-p026-07.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SpecConstant.to: Each constant constructor produces one syntax token of the corresponding kind and passes through its payload. For example, a hexadecimal constant passes its digit sequence, since the lexical-to-syntax conversion has already dropped `#x`.

2-7-p026-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Syntax.IsSExpr: Start by bracketing `(assert x)` as a list with two atoms, the reserved word `assert` and the symbol `x`. The same rule reads `(a (b 1))` as a list with atom `a` and a nested list. `IsSExpr` checks that a tree is valid in the selected version and that writing it back gives exactly the supplied tokens. Here the grouping already works before the script supplies a declaration for `x`.
2-7-p026-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SExpr.Valid: Of the four atom alternatives, only the reserved-word case has a further condition here. It checks that the version is at least 2.6 and that the word belongs to that version. The list case repeats the check at every depth.
2-7-p026-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SExpr: The four non-list constructors identify which kind of atom the production places at a leaf. In `(a (b 1))`, the outer `.list` stores two items, a `.symbol` for `a` and a second `.list`. The second list stores a symbol and a numeral constant. Because `.list` takes a `List SExpr`, each item can itself contain a list, and the empty list is the tree for `()`.
2-7-p026-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SExpr.tokens: Each atom branch produces a singleton list in its own token category. The `.list` branch concatenates the members' tokens inside parentheses, preserving the nesting of the displayed production.

2-7-p027-02.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Identifier.toke: For an identifier with indices, `Identifier.tokens` emits `(`, the reserved token `_`, the symbol, its index tokens in order, and `)`. A symbol with an empty index list is emitted on its own.
2-7-p027-02.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Index.tokens: Each index contributes one token to the enclosing identifier. For example, the final component of `(_ BitVec 32)` is a numeral token with payload `32`.

2-7-p027-03.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Index.Valid: Both alternatives satisfy `Index.Valid` in version 2.7. The version check is relevant to symbolic indices, which this implementation admits from 2.5 onward. The characters of a numeral or symbol are handled by the lexicon.
2-7-p027-03.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Index: The alternatives on either side of the bar are the two constructors of `Index`. A numeral index stores the digits, while a symbol index stores a `Symbol`, including its quoting flag.
2-7-p027-03.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Index.tokens: The two cases write one `.numeral` or one `.symbol` syntax token with the supplied payload. The underscore that introduces an indexed identifier belongs to the surrounding identifier, outside the index itself.

2-7-p027-04.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Identifier.Vali: An identifier stores a symbol together with its list of indices. `Identifier.Valid` applies `Index.Valid` to every entry in that list. For `(_ extract 7 4)` it checks the two numeral indices, and the predicate also admits symbolic indices starting with version 2.5. The bare identifier `extract` has an empty list and passes this check immediately. `Identifier.tokens` supplies the grammar's other constraint by writing the parenthesized underscore form only for a nonempty list.
2-7-p027-04.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Identifier: Both sides of the production use one Lean structure with a symbol and a list of indices. Empty indices encode the plain alternative and a populated list encodes the indexed alternative.
2-7-p027-04.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Identifier.toke: With symbol `extract` and numeral indices `7` and `4`, the writer emits `(_ extract 7 4)`. Each index contributes its own token in list order. With an empty index list, the writer gives the bare identifier `extract`, as the first alternative of the production requires.

2-7-p027-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Attribute.token: A value of `none` yields the keyword alone. With `some value`, `Attribute.tokens` prepends the keyword to the tokens of that value. There is no additional wrapper for the attribute as a whole.
The branches correspond to the production below the paragraph. They emit a constant, a symbol, or a parenthesized list of S-expressions. A reserved word can appear inside the list if grammatically valid, while the listed branches have no bare reserved-word case.

Only a value in the list branch needs a further grammar check here. `SExpr.ValidAll` checks its members, including the version's restrictions on reserved-word atoms. The two atomic forms satisfy this predicate directly.
2-7-p027-09.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.AttributeValue: The type has one case for each alternative in the production. Its third case contains a list of S-expressions and permits an empty list, represented in the grammar as `()`.
The constant and symbol branches each emit one token. The list branch emits the members' tokens inside parentheses, even for an empty list. The attribute keyword is emitted separately by `Attribute.tokens`.

2-7-p027-10.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Syntax.IsAttribute: For a supplied token list, `IsAttribute` requires an exact match with the attribute's tokens and grammatical validity of its optional value. The keyword's spelling belongs to the preceding lexical stage.
2-7-p027-10.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Attribute.Valid: The keyword-only branch is `True`. The branch with a value calls `AttributeValue.Valid` in the same version, leaving any restrictions tied to a particular attribute name to the context where it is used.
2-7-p027-10.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Attribute: In `:named a`, the keyword names the attribute and `a` is its symbol value. A keyword alone can also be an attribute under this production. Lean's `Option AttributeValue` records exactly this choice, leaving rules about what particular attribute names require to their contexts.
2-7-p027-10.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Attribute.token: Begin with the keyword token. For an attribute stored with `none`, such as the grammar shape `:flag`, that token is the entire output. For `:named claim`, the structure stores `some` symbol value and `Attribute.tokens` appends its tokens immediately after `:named`. The value supplies any grouping of its own. The two alternatives in the passage therefore produce the same leading token and differ in what follows it.

2-7-p028-02.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Sort.tokens: In these grammar rules, a sort expression such as `Bool` is written as its identifier alone. An application such as `(Array Int Bool)` adds parentheses and writes the argument sorts in order. This operation starts from a given sort tree, so assigning a sort to a term is a separate question.

2-7-p028-03.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Syntax.IsSort: For `(Array Int Real)`, start at the `Array` node, then check the two child sorts `Int` and `Real` and write the tree back to compare tokens. `(Array Int)` also has the grammatical shape of a sort. The signature supplies the requirement that `Array` take two arguments.
2-7-p028-03.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Sort.Valid: For each sort node, `Valid` checks the identifier's indices and recursively checks the argument subtrees. The predicate has no signature parameter for checking declared arities.
2-7-p028-03.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Sort: The only constructor contains an identifier and a recursive list of sort arguments. The identifier alone in the first alternative is the case with an empty argument list.
2-7-p028-03.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Sort.tokens: The branch for zero arguments writes the bare identifier. A populated argument list yields `(`, the identifier and each argument's tokens, then `)`, so the parenthesized form contains at least one argument.

2-7-p030-01.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.Valid: In the application case, `Valid` requires at least one argument and checks the qualified identifier and each argument for grammatical validity. The predicate has no binder environment or function signature, so variables and function ranks are resolved outside this check.
For the passage's final form, the `.as` case emits `as`, the tokens of $f$ and the tokens of $\tau$ between parentheses. The plain case emits the identifier's tokens alone.
2-7-p030-01.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.tokens: Write `x` on its own, then write it again as the body in `(let ((x 1)) x)`. Both occurrences are emitted by the same identifier branch. The enclosing `let` introduces the binder in the second case. This is why a written identifier alone gives only the spelling, while its context determines whether it refers to a binder.

`Valid` checks the identifier in both alternatives. In the `.as` branch it also checks the sort expression. Both checks are grammatical and use the selected version.
2-7-p030-02.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.QualIdentifier: In a list datatype, a writer can qualify `nil` with an intended result sort by writing `(as nil (List Int))`. The grammar stores `nil` alone as `.plain identifier`. For the `as` form, `.as identifier sort` stores the same kind of identifier plus a structured sort expression. Here that expression has `List` as its head and `Int` as its argument. The constructor records the explicit sort, which later checks can compare with the declaration of `nil`.
The plain branch uses `Identifier.tokens`. The qualified branch uses `paren` to enclose the reserved word `as`, the identifier tokens and the sort tokens in that order.

2-7-p030-03.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.ValidBindi: The production describes one binding, which Lean stores as a symbol–term pair. The list helper checks the term in every pair and succeeds on an empty list. The enclosing `let` rule requires a nonempty list.
2-7-p030-03.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.bindingTok: In `(let ((x 1)) x)`, the pair `(x 1)` is one binding, `((x 1))` is the list of bindings, and the final `x` is the body. `bindingTokens` adds the parentheses around each pair. The `let` branch adds the outer list parentheses, so a reader can tell where the binding list ends and the body begins.

2-7-p030-04.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SortedVar.Valid: Only the sort component of a sorted variable is checked here. This amounts to checking the grammar of the sort and its arguments, independently of how the variable name will be used.
2-7-p030-04.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SortedVar: Read `(x Int)` as a declaration of the name `x` with sort `Int`. `SortedVar` represents exactly that pair, with a `Symbol` in its `symbol` field and a sort tree in its `sort` field. The same pair can appear in a binder's variable list or in a function's parameter list. The enclosing construct supplies the scope in which occurrences of `x` refer to that declaration.
2-7-p030-04.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SortedVar.token: For a pair such as `(x Int)`, the name supplies one symbol token and the sort supplies its own tokens. `paren` groups them as one sorted variable.

2-7-p030-05.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SymbolOrWildcar: Inside a pattern, bare `_` is the `.wildcard` alternative. The validity test for that constructor requires `versionAtLeast version .v2_7`. This is a check on the use of the reserved token in a pattern, so the earlier use of `_` to introduce an indexed identifier does not enable it. Quoted `|_|` goes through the `.symbol` alternative, for which this predicate is `True`.
An ordinary name yields a symbol token and the wildcard yields the reserved token `_`. A quoted symbol such as `|_|` still uses the symbol branch.

2-7-p030-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Pattern.Valid: In 2.7, `(cons h _)` has a constructor name followed by two arguments, one named and one wildcard. `(cons)` has an empty argument list and fails this branch's check. A nullary constructor pattern is written as a bare symbol, such as `nil`. The datatype declaration determines whether that symbol names a constructor.
2-7-p030-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SymbolOrWildcar: This is the check for each occurrence of the grammar's symbol-or-wildcard category. In a constructor pattern it applies to arguments, while the constructor name itself is stored as a symbol.
2-7-p030-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Pattern: The `.single` branch contains a symbol or wildcard. The `.constructor` branch stores a constructor name and a list of symbol-or-wildcard arguments, with the requirement of at least one argument imposed by `Pattern.Valid`.
2-7-p030-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SymbolOrWildcar: Lean uses the same two-constructor type for a pattern consisting of one item and for each argument of a parenthesized constructor pattern. Only the `.symbol` branch stores a name.
2-7-p030-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Pattern.tokens: The single case emits one token. The constructor case emits the name and then each argument token inside parentheses. An empty argument list can still be written by this function, so validity supplies the plus in the production.
2-7-p030-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SymbolOrWildcar: The one-token conversion is used both for a pattern consisting of a single item and for arguments after a constructor name. The parentheses in the latter case are added by `Pattern.tokens`.

2-7-p030-07.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.ValidCases: For each pattern–term pair the helper requires both parts to be valid in the selected version. The base case is `True`, so the enclosing `match` case of `Term.Valid` supplies the requirement that at least one case exists.
2-7-p030-07.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.caseTokens: For one pair, the function emits the pattern followed by the result term inside parentheses, as in the production. Across several pairs it repeats that operation and concatenates the output in order.

2-7-p030-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Syntax.IsTerm: A tree with application head `f` and an empty argument list can emit `(f)`, yet the production requires at least one argument. `IsTerm` therefore checks both the emitted tokens and `Term.Valid`. A tree for `(f x)` passes the application-list check, and the bare identifier form `f` has its own branch.
2-7-p030-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.Valid: Each plus in the term production has a corresponding nonempty-list test for that form. Lean also requires version 2.6 for `match` and 2.7 for `lambda`, and it checks the component terms in the same version.
2-7-p030-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term: The two quantifier productions share a `.quantified` constructor whose first field chooses `forall` or `exists`. Other forms have their own constructors. Their list fields can be empty at this stage, with the grammar's nonempty tests in `Term.Valid`.
2-7-p030-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.tokens: The branches assemble the printed forms out of syntax tokens, including the inner parentheses around repeated bindings, variables and cases. They can emit such lists even when empty, with the plus requirements checked by `Term.Valid`.
2-7-p030-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Quantifier.word: The quantified-term branch uses this function to choose its leading reserved token, `forall` or `exists`. Both choices use the same code for the variable list and the body.

2-7-p031-02.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.Valid: For a binder such as `let`, `Valid` checks the grammar of the bindings and the body. Free and bound occurrences are described separately in the standard, and no assignment from names to their binders appears in this predicate.
2-7-p031-02.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.tokens: The token function preserves the written positions of binders, names and bodies. For example it emits a `let` binding list before the body. The standard gives separate scope rules for identifying the occurrences that refer to each binding.

2-7-p031-03.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.Valid: In `(lambda ((x Int) (y Int)) x)`, the two declarations occupy one list in the syntax tree. The standard interprets the list as nesting, first binding `x` and then `y`. `Term.Valid` accepts the list form in 2.7 after checking the body and both sort expressions, and rejects the empty list in `(lambda () x)`.
2-7-p031-03.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.tokens: A lambda node with two variables becomes a single `lambda` followed by a list with two entries and then the body. These are the tokens of the abbreviated form in (3.1) before the expansion written in (3.2).

2-7-p031-07.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.Valid: Both quantifiers use the same check for a nonempty list of sorted variables and a grammatically valid body. The standard's expansion into nested quantifiers belongs to the interpretation of the resulting expression.
2-7-p031-07.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SortedVar.token: Each quantified variable contributes a group such as `(x Int)`. The quantified-term branch collects the groups into one variable list before the body, as in the unexpanded form described here.

2-7-p032-10.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.Valid: In `(match l ((nil 0) ((cons h t) h)))`, `l` is the term being matched and the two pairs give its cases. In 2.7, `Term.Valid` can check both pairs and the shape of `l` from their syntax. A datatype declaration is needed to tell whether `nil` and `cons` are constructors of the sort of `l`.
2-7-p032-10.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.tokens: The `match` branch writes the term to be matched first, then a parenthesized list of cases in order. The function emits this syntax for a given tree. Selecting a case is part of evaluation.

2-7-p033-01.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Pattern.Valid: The predicate checks that a constructor pattern has arguments and that each argument is allowed in the version. A single symbol satisfies the same check whether it denotes a variable or a nullary constructor. That distinction and the rank conditions depend on the datatype declaration.
2-7-p033-01.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.ValidCases: The helper checks each pair's pattern and result term separately. There is no datatype or expected result sort among its inputs, so coverage of the datatype and agreement of result sorts lie outside the check.
2-7-p033-01.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Pattern.tokens: A lone variable or nullary constructor is emitted as one symbol token, and a wildcard as `_`. In the constructor branch the head and the argument tokens appear inside parentheses. The encoding records the syntax before any checks on ranks or bound variables.

2-7-p033-05.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Pattern: In `(cons h t)`, each argument is a name, and so each fits `SymbolOrWildcard`. In `(cons h (cons k t))`, the second argument would have to hold an entire pattern. The argument type has no constructor for that tree, which enforces the flatness of patterns directly.
2-7-p033-05.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Pattern.tokens: After the constructor name, `Pattern.tokens` maps a one-token function over the arguments. There is no recursive call for an argument, reflecting the flat constructor patterns described in the remark.

2-7-p033-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Identifier.toke: In `(_ BitVec 32)`, the `_` is emitted once before the identifier's symbol and indices. Its position in the parenthesized group identifies this use as indexing.
2-7-p033-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Pattern.tokens: In `(cons x _)`, the tree's head is the constructor name `cons` and its two arguments are a symbol and a wildcard. `Pattern.tokens` writes the head followed by one token for each argument inside parentheses. The wildcard contributes the same reserved token `_` that introduces `(_ BitVec 32)`, but it appears in an argument position here. A sole wildcard pattern is the `.single` branch and writes just `_`.
2-7-p033-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SymbolOrWildcar: The wildcard branch produces the same reserved token spelling `_` that occurs in an indexed identifier. Which use it has depends on the grammar surrounding that token.

In the `.as` case, `Valid` asks whether $f$ is a grammatically valid identifier and $\tau$ a grammatically valid sort expression. The remark's requirement that $\tau$ match a declared result sort needs the function's rank as well.

The function can write a supplied identifier and sort in the `as` form without looking up the identifier. It accounts for the spelling in the remark, where the required agreement with the declared return sort is a semantic condition.

2-7-p036-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.Valid: The annotation case requires a valid inner term and at least one grammatically valid attribute. The standard also assigns the wrapper the same logical meaning as its inner term. `Valid` only checks the grammar of the wrapper.
2-7-p036-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Term.tokens: With `p` a Boolean term, `(! p :named claim)` has the same logical meaning as `p`. The `.annotated` branch retains `!`, the term and the attribute in the token sequence. A tool that reads it back can recover the label `claim` as well as the inner term.

2-7-p050-04.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Script: If reading starts in 2.7, `(set-info :smt-lib-version 2.6)` is itself read in 2.7. The next command is read in 2.6. `Script.command` passes that resulting version to the rest of the list, so command validity is checked in the version in force at each position.
2-7-p050-04.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Command.tokens: With logic `QF_UF`, read `(declare-const x Bool)`, `(assert x)` and `(check-sat)` in order. The declaration supplies the sort of `x`, and setting `x` to true satisfies the assertion. Move the declaration after the assertion and `x` is undeclared when first used. `Command.tokens` prints the same `(assert x)` in both orders, and prints `(check-sat)` as a command with zero arguments.

2-7-p051-01.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SortDec: In a `declare-datatypes` sort declaration, `SortDec` stores a symbol and the arity's numeral as bytes. The `arity` field holds that spelling directly, without first converting it to a Lean natural number.
2-7-p051-01.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SortDec.tokens: The name and arity produce a symbol token and a numeral token inside one pair of parentheses. For example, a declaration of arity one for `List` produces the tokens of `(List 1)`.

2-7-p051-02.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SelectorDec.Val: At this point the selector already has a symbol and a sort. `Valid` calls the grammar predicate on the sort in the selected version. The datatype declaration supplies the context in which the selector name is introduced.
2-7-p051-02.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SelectorDec: In the list constructor declaration `(cons (car T) (cdr (List T)))`, the two inner pairs declare selectors. The first names `car` and gives it result sort `T`. The second names `cdr` and gives it the sort `(List T)`. Each pair becomes a `SelectorDec` with fields `symbol` and `sort`. The enclosing `ConstructorDec` stores those two selector declarations in order.
2-7-p051-02.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SelectorDec.tok: The selector contributes its name as one symbol token, then the tokens of its result sort. The enclosing pair of parentheses marks off that selector from other selectors in a constructor.

For `(nil)` the selector list is empty, so the requirement that each selector be valid holds immediately. That is the zero-repetition case of the star in this production. For `(cons (car T) (cdr (List T)))`, the predicate checks both selectors in the selected version, including the recursive sort expression `(List T)` of the second. Whether the surrounding datatype actually declares `T` is checked when interpreting that declaration.
2-7-p051-03.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.ConstructorDec: The name field represents the leading symbol, and the list field represents the repeated selector declarations. A nullary constructor uses the case with an empty selector list.
`ConstructorDec.tokens` starts with the name, appends the already grouped tokens of each selector, and encloses the result. For a nullary constructor such as `nil`, this leaves just `(nil)`.

2-7-p051-04.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.DatatypeDec.Val: The nonempty constructor condition supplies the plus shared by both alternatives. The same predicate checks the grammar of every constructor. Sort parameters and constructor arities are checked against the surrounding declarations when interpreting the datatype.
2-7-p051-04.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.DatatypeDec: The `List` example has a type parameter `T` and constructors `nil` and `cons`. It uses the `par` form to put `(T)` before the constructor list. `DatatypeDec` stores both lists, and an empty parameter list writes the simpler form without `par`.
2-7-p051-04.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.DatatypeDec.tok: With no parameters the function encloses the constructors in one list. With parameters it emits the `par` wrapper with separate parameter and constructor groups. The function can write an empty constructor group, which the validity predicate excludes.

2-7-p051-05.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.FunctionDec.Val: The check requires each parameter's sort and the result sort to be grammatical in the selected version. The star permits zero parameters, and the assertion over the parameter list holds vacuously in that case.
2-7-p051-05.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.FunctionDec: The structure stores a name, a list of named parameters with their sorts, and the result sort. A `define-funs-rec` node stores these declarations separately from the associated body terms.
2-7-p051-05.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.FunctionDec.tok: The inner parentheses enclose the sorted variable list, even when it is empty. The outer pair groups the name, parameter list and result sort into a declaration that can be one entry in `define-funs-rec`.

2-7-p051-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.FunctionDef.Val: The check calls `Valid` on each sorted parameter, the stated result sort and the body. Grammatical validity of the body is a separate condition from having the declared result sort.
2-7-p051-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.FunctionDef: In `(define-fun id ((x Int)) Int x)`, the `FunctionDef` begins at `id`. Its `symbol` is the function name, `parameters` contains the single `SortedVar` for `(x Int)`, `result` stores the sort `Int`, and `body` stores the term `x`. The earlier occurrence of `x` is a parameter declaration and the final one is an identifier term. The command constructor supplies `define-fun` and the outer parentheses, and `define-fun-rec` uses the same four-field definition.
2-7-p051-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.FunctionDef.tok: Only the parameter list gets its own parentheses in this function. It emits the name, that list, the result sort and then the body. The wrapper for `define-fun` or `define-fun-rec` is added by the command branch.

2-7-p051-07.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Syntax.IsCommand: The pinned examples read `(check-sat-assuming (p (not q)))` as a list of terms in 2.7 and as a list of propositional literals in 2.6. Both trees write the same tokens. The version argument to `IsCommand` determines which tree satisfies the grammar.
2-7-p051-07.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Command.Valid: In `define-funs-rec`, every declared function needs a body in the corresponding position of the second list. Two declarations and only one body still fit the tree's list fields, but `Command.Valid` rejects that tree by requiring equal lengths and a nonempty declaration list. It also checks the recursive syntax of the declarations and bodies. The same paired-length check appears for `declare-datatypes`. The selected version matters separately, for example when choosing the term or literal form of `check-sat-assuming`.
2-7-p051-07.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Command: Each command is stored with the arguments named in its production. The type also stores a separate `check-sat-assuming` form for the older grammar, and stores the two lists of `define-funs-rec` independently until validity is checked.
2-7-p051-07.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Command.tokens: `commandTokens` wraps each command name and the tokens of its arguments. The branch for `define-funs-rec`, for example, writes one group of declarations and a second group of bodies. Equal lengths are checked by `Command.Valid`.

2-7-p051-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Script: Read `(check-sat) (exit)` from left to right. The first command leaves the reading version in place, and the second ends the list. Reversing their order fails to make a two-command `Script`, because the stopping constructor requires the last command to stand alone.

2-7-p052-02.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Attribute.token: A named option like `:random-seed 17` uses the value-bearing case, with a keyword and a numeral token. The final alternative in the production admits the general attribute form, which this function also writes with no value when the field is `none`.
2-7-p052-02.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Command.tokens: The `set-option` branch writes its argument using `Attribute.tokens`. It uses the same branch for a predefined name such as `:produce-models` and a solver-specific option. The meaning of each option is specified separately.

2-7-p052-04.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Command.tokens: The `get-info` case puts one keyword token after the command name. Because the production ends with the general keyword alternative, the function needs no separate cases for flags such as `:version` or `:name`.

2-7-p052-06.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Command.tokens: The token function writes `(get-info :time)` by the same rule it uses for `(get-info :name)`. The choice of flag changes the keyword payload. Whether that flag is supported and what the solver returns are questions about execution.

2-7-p104-01.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.reserved: Predefined spellings such as `Bool`, `true` and `sat` are absent from both lists supplied to `litOneOf` at version 2.7. Their special meanings are distinct from whether the lexer classifies them as reserved words.
2-7-p104-01.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.simpleSymbol: The listed names pass the simple-symbol spelling test at version 2.7. For example, the hyphen in `continued-execution` is allowed punctuation and the complete name is outside the reserved-word set. The rule applies before the name is assigned a meaning.

2-7-p104-03.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.whiteSpaceChar: Each decimal code in the appendix becomes one `code` alternative in `whiteSpaceChar`. These are byte values $9$, $10$, $13$ and $32$, with comments handled by the separate whitespace rule.

2-7-p104-04.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.printableChar: The two runs in the appendix coincide with the two inclusive byte ranges in `printableChar`. The alternatives include $126$ and $128$ but skip $127$.

2-7-p104-05.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.digit: The appendix writes the glyphs `0` through `9`, and `range 48 57` uses their ASCII byte values. Each match contains a single byte.

2-7-p104-06.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.letter: The alphabet here matches the two branches of `letter`. They use the inclusive ASCII intervals $65$ to $90$ for uppercase and $97$ to $122$ for lowercase.

2-7-p105-03.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.numeral: The two parts of the appendix rule become an alternation with `lit "0"` and a subtraction from `plus digit`. The subtraction removes digit sequences that begin with `0`, so only the first branch can accept `0`.

2-7-p105-04.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.decimal: `seq` joins a numeral, the literal point, the starred run of zeroes, and another numeral. That is why `1.00` has the required final digit even though its fractional digits are all zero.

2-7-p105-05.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.hexadecimal: The expression starts with the fixed literal `#x`. The disjunction inside `plus` is where capital and lowercase letters are both accepted, for as many hex digits as follow the prefix.

2-7-p105-06.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.binary: `lit "#b"` fixes the prefix and `plus` requires at least one byte from `oneOf "01"`. Every unit after the prefix is a single binary digit.

2-7-p105-07.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.string: The outer two `lit` expressions match the delimiters. Each repetition inside them consumes a permitted byte other than a quote or two quotes together, so the pair counts as one unit of the interior.
2-7-p105-07.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.unescape: The appendix names the escape `""`. In Lean the two-quote branch consumes both bytes and copies one quote to the result. The surrounding delimiter quotes have already been removed when `Token.content` calls this function.

2-7-p105-08.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.simpleSymbol: The rest of the production lists the punctuation and excludes a digit at the start and a reserved word as the complete spelling. Lean first forms the nonempty sequence with `plus`, then applies those two exclusions.
2-7-p105-08.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.symbolPunctuation: The characters listed in the continuation fill the literal passed to `oneOf`. Any one of them may occur within a candidate simple symbol, subject to the rule for the complete name.

2-7-p105-09.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.quotedSymbol: The second alternative is the bar-delimited one. `quotedSymbol` matches an empty interior or a sequence of white space and printable bytes after removing the two forbidden interior characters, the bar and backslash.
2-7-p105-09.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.simpleSymbol: The first alternative calls for a simple symbol, whose spelling is checked against `simpleSymbol` in the selected version. For example, `abc` uses this regular expression and `|abc|` uses the bar-delimited expression.

2-7-p105-10.BSmtLibSpec.Lexicon.keyword: The appendix refers to the entire simple-symbol rule after the colon. Lean instead calls for a nonempty letter, digit or punctuation sequence. It therefore admits `:56` and `:let`, following the older rule documented beside `keyword`.

2-7-p106-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Pattern.Valid: Compare the plus in the appendix with `arguments ≠ []` in the constructor branch. The remaining test checks each argument in the selected version, including whether a wildcard is available.
2-7-p106-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SymbolOrWildcar: The metavariable `symbol_` marks a position that can hold a wildcard. `Valid` accepts the symbol case unconditionally and the wildcard case from 2.7 onward.
2-7-p106-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Pattern: The appendix's two alternatives correspond to `.single` and `.constructor`. The constructor's argument field is an ordinary list, with the plus in the appendix enforced by the separate grammar predicate.
2-7-p106-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SymbolOrWildcar: A bare pattern or a constructor argument can contain a value of this type. Its two alternatives are a named symbol and a wildcard, which is why the constructor arguments in this representation are flat.
2-7-p106-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.Pattern.tokens: The single case emits one token and the constructor case writes the head and argument tokens inside parentheses. `Pattern.Valid` rules out a constructor spelling with only the head.
2-7-p106-08.BSmtLibSpec.Grammar.Tree.SymbolOrWildcar: Each occurrence of `symbol_` in the production contributes one token, either the supplied symbol or the reserved `_`. The outer pattern branch decides whether that token stands alone or occurs among constructor arguments.
